title: What is Software Testing & Why Teams Test
summary: The disciplined process of evaluating software to uncover discrepancies and mitigate release risk.
meaning: Testing is empirical investigation conducted to provide stakeholders with objective information about product quality and behavioral risks.
importance: Without rigorous testing, fatal crashes, security vulnerabilities, or broken game economies reach real players, damaging studio reputation.
example: In a multiplayer shooter, QA validates that collision geometry stops players from walking through mountain walls to gain an unfair advantage.
action: Observe games you play: notice subtle edge conditions like pausing right as a dialogue trigger starts.

title: QA vs. Testing
summary: Process-oriented quality assurance vs. execution-oriented defect identification.
meaning: QA focuses on standards, processes, and continuous improvement to prevent defects from being injected into the pipeline. Testing is the tactical execution of the product to find existing defects.
importance: Having testing without QA means you continually fight fires; having QA without testing means you never empirically inspect the software.
example: QA establishes coding guidelines and automated build validation. Testing executes a 2-hour stress test on Android builds.
action: Evaluate your own workflow: do you check requirements before starting, or solely inspect after writing code?

title: Error, Defect (Bug), and Failure
summary: The fundamental chain of human mistake, code flaw, and observable runtime breakdown.
meaning: An Error is a human mistake made by a programmer or designer. A Defect (bug) is the flaw remaining in the software artifact. A Failure is the unintended event experienced when the flawed code executes.
importance: Distinguishing these prevents blaming players for unexpected behaviors and helps developers locate root causes quickly.
example: Error: Dev writes `if (hp = 0)` instead of `==`. Defect: Assignment replaces comparison. Failure: Player immediately dies upon taking 1 point of damage.
action: When encountering an anomaly, trace backwards from the symptom (failure) to where logic might have slipped.

title: Verification vs. Validation
summary: Building the product right (verification) vs. building the right product (validation).
meaning: Verification asks: 'Did we build the game according to specifications?'. Validation asks: 'Does the game satisfy the real player's expectations and needs?'.
importance: A game can pass 100% of specification checks (Verification) while still feeling confusing or unpleasant to play (Validation).
example: Verification: Jumping velocity exactly matches the 12.5 m/s spec. Validation: Playtesters report that jumping feels sluggish and floats unrealistically.
action: When testing a feature, first check the design doc, then step back and ask: 'Does this actually feel satisfying?'.

title: Equivalence Partitioning & Boundary Value Analysis
summary: Dividing input domains into valid/invalid subsets and testing their exact edges.
meaning: Equivalence groups assume values in the same partition produce identical logic. Boundary testing validates the minimum and maximum edges where comparisons flip.
importance: You cannot test billions of input combinations. Boundary analysis provides maximum defect-finding power in minimal time.
example: Level limits 1-50. Equivalence sets: Invalid negative, Valid (1-50), Invalid (>50). Boundaries tested: 0, 1, 50, 51.
action: List the boundaries for a high-score leaderboard displaying ranks 1 through 100.

title: Exploratory Testing & Charters
summary: Simultaneous learning, test design, and test execution guided by a clear mission charter.
meaning: Unlike rigid scripted checklists, exploratory testing gives skilled testers freedom to investigate anomalies using structured time-boxed charters.
importance: Scripted tests only find what was anticipated. Exploratory testing uncovers unexpected emergent behaviors in complex games.
example: Charter: 'Explore character inventory switching during rapid network latency to discover item duplication defects within 45 minutes.'
action: Pick a mobile game menu and explore it for 15 minutes with the express mission of interrupting animations.

title: State-Transition & Decision Tables
summary: Mapping out game entity states (Alive, Stunned, Dead) and input condition combinations.
meaning: A state machine ensures entities only move between legal states. Decision tables map complex multi-variable business rules into a grid.
example: Can a player cast a spell while 'Stunned'? State table shows Stunned -> Cast is an illegal transition.
action: Draw a simple state transition diagram for an in-game shopping cart: Empty -> Populated -> Checkout -> Completed.

title: Risk-Based Testing
summary: Prioritizing testing effort based on defect likelihood and severity of impact.
meaning: When release deadlines approach, QA focuses on high-risk features (payment transactions, core progression saves) over low-risk cosmetics.
example: Focusing 80% of test cycles on in-app purchase receipts rather than the credit roll typography.
action: Rank 3 features by risk: In-app store, Options volume slider, and Single-player save loading.

title: Severity vs. Priority
summary: Technical impact on the system vs. urgency of business scheduling.
meaning: Severity is determined primarily by QA based on how badly the product is impaired. Priority is set by product leadership based on release readiness and user impact.
importance: Conflating severity and priority causes developers to patch minor edge-case crashes instead of release-blocking visual typos.
example: A spelling typo on the startup title screen: Low Severity, High Priority (damages immediate first impression).
action: Practice classifying real bugs into 2x2 grids: High/Low Severity vs. High/Low Priority.

title: Evidence & Privacy-Safe Reporting
summary: Attaching logs, screenshots, and videos without leaking sensitive user identifiers.
meaning: High-quality bug reports require concrete evidence (logs, timestamps). Testers must ensure no private account tokens, emails, or PII are exposed in screenshots.
importance: Protects privacy compliance while providing developers visual proof of reproduction steps.
example: Blurring out test player email addresses or payment card tokens in QA video attachments.
action: Inspect bug reports to confirm screenshots only display test accounts in sandbox environments.

title: Retest, Regression, Smoke, and Sanity
summary: Understanding the four key execution cycles in agile and release testing.
meaning: Smoke test: quick broad check that build runs. Sanity test: focused check that specific subsystem works. Retest: confirming a bug is resolved. Regression: confirming nothing else broke.
importance: Executing full test suites for every tiny hotfix is impossible; distinct test passes optimize QA bandwidth.
example: Smoke test: Launch game, reach main menu, start tutorial. Takes 5 minutes.
action: Design a 3-step smoke test for your favorite phone application.

title: Test Execution Statuses: Pass, Fail, Blocked, Not Run
summary: Standard reporting statuses used in studio test management tools.
meaning: Pass: behavior matches specification. Fail: defect identified. Blocked: an external bug prevents executing the step. Not Run: test pending execution.
importance: Clear statuses provide team leads with real-time visibility into actual test velocity and bottlenecks.
example: If a door cannot be opened due to a missing key, any test case evaluating the dungeon behind it is marked 'Blocked'.
action: Never mark a test 'Pass' if you skipped any precondition or prerequisite step.
